title: Lace cowl
subtitle: A simple eyelet repeat worked in the round on 4 mm needles.
excerpt: A cowl knitted in the round in a four-row eyelet lace repeat on 4 mm needles with DK-weight yarn, finishing at 56 cm circumference and 28 cm tall. The lace repeat uses paired yarn-overs and k2tog decreases worked on every fourth round, with all other rounds knitted plain. The result is a regular grid of eyelets across the full tube.
sourceNotes: Eyelet lace on circular needles for neckwear appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. Simple repeat-based lace in the round is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only.
heroPrompt: A finished lace cowl in pale blue DK yarn, worn around the neck showing the regular eyelet grid pattern around the full circumference, photographed against a plain light background.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wrapping the working yarn over the right needle between stitches to create a new stitch and an eyelet. In the round between two knit stitches, this is a simple forward loop over the needle tip.
Knit two stitches together as one. Right-leaning decrease, used here to balance each yarn-over.
Knitting a small circumference on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the work at the halfway point, dividing stitches into two groups on the two needle tips.
Soaking the finished piece in cool water, pressing out excess water, and pinning to the stated dimensions on a flat surface until fully dry. Opens lace eyelets.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a cowl knitted in the round in a four-round eyelet lace repeat on 4 mm needles with DK-weight yarn, finishing at 56 cm circumference and 28 cm tall after blocking. Each
yarn-over
is paired with a
k2tog

in the same round, working on every fourth round with three plain knit rounds in between. The eyelets autumn in a staggered grid pattern across the tube when the 4-stitch repeat is offset by two stitches between eyelet rounds.
In-the-round construction was chosen because a seamless tube allows the eyelet pattern to travel continuously around the circumference without a seam interrupting the repeat. The
magic loop
method on a 80 cm circular needle is the recommended approach. The finished cowl needs about 280 m (approximately 100 g) of DK-weight yarn and sits as a loose ring around the neck and collarbone.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or wool-silk blend
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight yarn. Wool or wool-silk blocks the eyelets open cleanly.

items.name: 4 mm circular needle, 80 cm (UK 8 / US 6)
items.substitutions: 60 cm also works if you prefer a short-cable method.

content.text: Gauge

22 sts x 28 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch in the round on 4 mm needles, blocked. In eyelet lace the gauge is approximately 20 sts per 10 cm because the yarn-overs widen the fabric slightly. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished circumference by approximately 2.8 cm at this stitch count. Round gauge drift across the 72 body rounds changes the finished height by up to 8 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn, draw loop through.
YO (yarn over): bring yarn over the right needle tip from front to back between two knit stitches. Creates one new stitch and one eyelet.
K2tog: insert right needle through two stitches together and knit as one. Right-leaning decrease. One stitch consumed, balancing the yarn-over.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 112 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is a multiple of 4 for the eyelet repeat: 112 = 28 x 4. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 4 mm needles (circumference approximately 12.6 mm) and 112 stitches: (12.6 x 112) / 10 + 15 = 141.1 + 15 = about 156 cm. Leave a tail of at least 156 cm; wind it loosely before the slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 112 stitches on the needle. Join to work in the round without twisting. Place a stitch marker.
Body
Rib section (6 rounds): *K1, P1; repeat from * to end. (112 sts)
Eyelet round A: *YO, K2tog, K2; repeat from * to end. (112 sts)
Rounds 2, 3, 4: K all stitches. (112 sts)
Eyelet round B (offset by 2 stitches): K2, *YO, K2tog, K2; repeat from * to last 2 sts, K2. (112 sts)
Rounds 6, 7, 8: K all stitches. (112 sts)

Repeat eyelet rounds A and B (each followed by 3 plain knit rounds) until the cowl body measures 26 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately round 36 of the body), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at round 36 of the body you should have 112 stitches on the needle.
Closing rib section (6 rounds): *K1, P1; repeat from * to end. (112 sts)
Bind off
Work a suspended bind-off on a knit round for a loose, open edge that matches the cast-on edge stretch.
Common faults

Eyelet rounds A and B landing in the same column rather than offset. Eyelet round B must begin with K2 before the repeat to shift the eyelets by two stitches relative to round A. If both rounds begin with YO, K2tog, the eyelets line up vertically instead of in a staggered grid.

Stitch count rising after an eyelet round. Each YO must be immediately followed by K2tog. Count the number of YO-K2tog pairs and confirm it equals 28 (the number of 4-stitch repeats in 112 stitches) at the end of every eyelet round.
Eyelets not opening before blocking. DK lace looks closed during knitting. Wet blocking opens the eyelets significantly. Always block before judging the lace success.
Finishing
Weave in both tails at the cast-on join and bind-off.
Wet blocking

opens the eyelets. Soak in cool water for 20 minutes, press out the water, and lay flat over a rounded form or folded towel to dry in the round shape. Pin the cast-on and bind-off edges gently to the stated circumference.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat over a round form to dry. Do not wring or stretch.
What to try next

The lace stole applies the same family of yarn-over and decrease lace tools to a flat wide piece in fingering-weight yarn. The helix-stripe cowl uses the same in-the-round construction with a colour change on every alternate round for a spiral stripe effect.
